name: Huberman sleep stack

lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime combination of magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, linked to neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. People use it to sleep better, which appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and looks.
Each ingredient is proposed to calm the nervous system by a different route. No published trial of the three-ingredient combination was found, and each ingredient has limited human sleep data.

paras: The three supplements are taken together in the evening before bed, usually as capsules or powder, and people judge it by sleep quality over days to weeks.
The ingredients are sold as supplements, which are loosely regulated, so quality varies. Critics of Huberman's supplement promotion say the claims go beyond what research shows.

angle.text: Popularized by a podcaster, this bedtime trio is used to improve sleep, which appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and a rested look. The combination has not been tested as a unit.

lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime supplement combination, commonly described as magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, associated with Stanford neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. It circulates in sleep and recovery discussions as a way to improve sleep, which some in appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and looks.

Andrew Huberman launched the Huberman Lab podcast in 2021 and has published the book Protocols [1]. Wikipedia reports that he promotes dietary supplements, which scientists have criticized, with one commentator describing the products as poorly regulated [1]. The sources reviewed here do not describe the specific stack, and no published trial of the three-ingredient combination as a unit was found.

paras: The stack is taken in the evening. Its components are individually sold as supplements; apigenin is a flavonoid found in chamomile, among other plants, and theanine is an amino acid found in tea. See the separate entries on magnesium threonate and on chamomile and passionflower tea for details on those ingredients.

Critics cited by Wikipedia have said Huberman's podcast sometimes presents certainty where evidence is ambiguous and applies animal research to humans without adequate justification [1]. Supporters regard his protocols as accessible summaries of neuroscience.
